description: Software developer (Ghaziabad, India) working on quantum-safe security for satellite communications. Building astronaut health monitoring software that spots risks early and sends health data to Earth with quantum-safe encryption. I bring backend dev, applied crypto and video production. Looking for: ML/data science, UI/UX design, health/physiology knowledge, and a great presenter. Let's build something real!
summary: CrewPulse gives astronauts a "body weather" forecast: today's health in one word, plus the next three days, learned from their own readings. A low-cost DIY chest band (about ₹3,500) streams ECG, heart rate, skin temperature and motion over Bluetooth to an app that works fully offline. It learns each astronaut's own normal, not Earth averages, counts irregular heartbeats, warns early about fever and stress, and gives a go / caution check before a spacewalk. We studied 20 medical incidents and risks from 1970 to 2026, from Apollo 15's skipped heartbeats to the first ISS medical evacuation: CrewPulse has a signal for 13 of them, and we openly show the 7 it can't cover yet. It matters because on a Mars mission Earth is up to 20 minutes away, so crews must notice and decide on board. Decision support only, not a medical device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

  • Body weather: fatigue, mood, heart, and muscle & bone, for today and the next 3 days, each with a plain "why" line. Tick a plan (for example, more sleep) and watch the forecast change.
  • Live Band: real heart rate, HRV, signal quality and a live ECG strip over Bluetooth. A labelled Demo Band simulator is built in.
  • Early Warning Index: four signals against your own baseline (irregular beats, resting heart rate, HRV, skin temperature). It flags "more irregular beats than your normal" (Apollo 15, Mir 1987 and 1997) or "your body may be fighting something" (Apollo 13, Salyut 7).
  • Daily 2-minute check-in: sleep, mood, stress, symptoms, grip strength, a vision self-check and a reaction-time test (the same idea as NASA's PVT).
  • Support: spots signs of strain and offers 2-minute paced breathing, showing heart rate and HRV before and after, plus a private request to talk to the crew medical officer.
  • Go / caution check before a spacewalk, docking or routine work, and a crew view for the crew medical officer.
  • Private report to ground: one daily report, encrypted in the browser (AES-256-GCM), sent only when the astronaut chooses. Post-quantum protection is planned; the app shows those steps as a labelled simulation.

HOW IT WORKS

  • The app is a Progressive Web App in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It installs on Android, Windows and Mac and runs with no internet. All data stays on the device.
  • Your normal is learned from your first 3 readings and is fully set after 14 days.
  • The Band: an ESP32-C3 board with an AD8232 ECG front end, a DS18B20 skin-temperature probe, an MPU6050 motion sensor, a vibration motor and a button on a chest belt. The firmware finds heartbeats on the board and sends compact packets over Bluetooth Low Energy.
  • Try it: the live app has a labelled sample-data mode (?sample) so every screen can be explored without a Band: https://shubhamsinha503.github.io/crewpulse/?sample

HOW NASA DATA SHAPED IT

NASA's astronaut medical records and Human Research Program evidence are the core of the design: they showed which signals warned first in real missions, which decided what the Band measures (ECG rhythm, resting heart rate, HRV, skin temperature), what the check-in asks, and the 13-of-20 incident coverage shown in the demo.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

  • We ran the app's own irregular-beat detector on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database: 44 recordings, 100,733 cardiologist-labelled beats. Precision is 92%: when it flags an early beat it is right 9 times in 10. It ranks people by irregular-beat load in nearly the right order (Spearman 0.83).
  • It misses about 2 in 3 irregular beats, so the app only reports change against your own normal, never absolute counts.
  • On the real Band we tested heart rate against wrist pulse, skin temperature against a warm hand, and motion at rest and when shaken.

HONEST LIMITS

  • Decision support only, not a medical device.
  • It can't detect toxic gas, CO₂, suit leaks, blood clots or bone loss: those need other sensors. There is no landing-readiness feature yet.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

  • Catches early, quiet changes (infection, strain, rhythm trouble, eye and muscle changes) and works without a link to Earth, keeping health data private to the astronaut.
  • Low cost and built in India: ready for missions like Gaganyaan, and for Mars.
  • On Earth, the same Band and app could support remote workers, polar stations and rural clinics.

TOOLS

  • Software: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Web Bluetooth, Web Crypto, Service Worker; Arduino C++ (ESP32-C3, NimBLE-Arduino, OneWire); Node.js for validation.
  • Hardware: ESP32-C3, AD8232, DS18B20, MPU6050, BC547 driver with a coin vibration motor.

DISCLOSURE

With our Local Lead's approval, we built a prototype of the app and the Band before the event. During the hackathon we finished it, tested it, published the code and the live app, made the demo and submitted.
